For solid aluminium facade panels, Metaguise uses 2.0 mm for residential and smaller exterior panels, 2.5 mm for primary exterior commercial facades, and 3.0 mm for high-wind-load locations and oversized formats. The right thickness depends on panel size, wind exposure, fixing method and how flat you want the face to look. Thickness should be set by the engineer for the project, not chosen on price alone.
Key takeaways

• Thicker is not always better. It adds weight and cost, so use what the load and panel size need. • Large panels and windy, tall sites need more thickness or stiffening. • Folded edges, ribs and sub-frame spacing can allow a thinner sheet. • Ask quotations to state the thickness, so you compare like with like.
Why panel thickness matters

Thickness affects four things you will notice: how flat the panel looks, how much it vibrates in wind, how well it resists dents, and how heavy it is for the sub-frame and installers. Thin panels can show waves, known as oil canning, especially on large flat areas in strong light. Thicker panels stay flatter but weigh and cost more.

It also affects honest comparison. A quote with a lower price per sq ft may use thinner sheet. Our guide to choosing a facade company notes that low bids may use thinner sheet, weaker coatings, or exclude scaffolding and sealants.

Panels have concealed mechanical fixings at the edges that engage an aluminium sub-frame. The standard shadow gap is 10 mm, with a 15 mm wide reveal as an option. Interior use usually specifies 2 mm gauge and a slimmer sub-frame, because wind load does not apply indoors.
What decides the right thickness

1. Wind load. Suction at edges and corners can govern. See our wind load guide for the engineering view. 2. Panel size. Bigger panels need more thickness, stiffeners or closer fixing. 3. Fixing and sub-frame spacing. Closer supports allow a thinner sheet. 4. Panel type. A cassette panel has folded return edges that add stiffness, so it can differ from a flat solid panel. See the cassette panel guide. 5. Finish and look. Dark, glossy or metallic finishes show waves more. 6. Building height and location. Taller, more exposed sites need more margin. 7. Budget and weight. Material cost rises with thickness, and so does load on the sub-frame.
Thickness for perforated and laser cut panels

Perforation removes material, so thickness, hole size and open area interact. A thin panel with many holes can lose stiffness. On the Nadaun indoor stadium project, a 2 mm perforated base layer sits behind laser-cut panels, with each system having its own weight and fixing method. Read the Nadaun stadium facade story. Questions to ask about thickness

• What thickness is in the quotation, and for which panel size? • Was it chosen from a wind load calculation? • How do you control flatness on large dark panels? • Is the sheet from a certified alloy, with mill certificates?
Our article on how facade panels are manufactured explains how sheet is checked on arrival and how forming tolerances are held.
Frequently asked questions

1. What thickness of aluminium is used for facade cladding?

Solid aluminium facade panels are commonly 2 to 3 mm. Metaguise uses 2.0 mm for residential and small panels, 2.5 mm for commercial facades and 3.0 mm for high-wind and oversized panels.

2. Is 3 mm aluminium better than 2 mm for a facade?

It is stiffer and suits larger or more exposed panels, but it is heavier and costs more. Choose what the panel size and wind load need.

3. Does thicker aluminium last longer?

Lifespan depends mostly on the finish, fixings and maintenance. Thickness mainly affects stiffness and flatness.

4. What is a solid panel in facade design?

It is a flat sheet aluminium panel, cut to size and fixed with concealed edge fixings, giving a smooth surface and narrow joints.

5. Can I use thinner panels to save money?

Only if the engineer confirms they meet the load and flatness requirements. Otherwise, savings can turn into waves, dents or fixing problems.

6. Do perforated panels need to be thicker?

Often they need careful design, because holes reduce stiffness. The engineer sets thickness, hole size and open area together.
